Modes: Three Meanings of One Word

What musicians mean by “mode” in Music Learning Theory (a tonality, heard from its resting tone), in classical theory (church modes and the major and minor modes) and in jazz (a scale chosen to fit one chord). The same notes, three answers.

You will hear the word mode used by three groups of musicians, and they don’t mean the same thing. A choir teacher trained in Music Learning Theory, a classical theory textbook and a jazz teacher can all look at the same notes and give three different answers to “what mode is this?” None of them is wrong. They are answering three different questions:

Who’s asking The question they mean Where the answer comes from
Music Learning Theory Which note does the music rest on, and how do the other notes feel around it? Your ear: the resting tone you audiate
Classical theory Which ordering of whole and half steps does this melody or piece use? The scale, its final (last note) and its history
Jazz Which scale fits this chord, right now? The chord symbol, one chord at a time

Click any heading to fold its section.

The shared starting point

All three begin with the same seven-note families. Play only the white keys of a piano and start and end on different notes, and you get the seven modes by their Greek names:

Start on Name Steps (W = whole, H = half) Compared with major on the same note
C Ionian (= major) W W H W W W H —
D Dorian W H W W W H W ♭3, ♭7
E Phrygian H W W W H W W ♭2, ♭3, ♭6, ♭7
F Lydian W W W H W W H ♯4
G Mixolydian W W H W W H W ♭7
A Aeolian (= natural minor) W H W W H W W ♭3, ♭6, ♭7
B Locrian H W W H W W W ♭2, ♭3, ♭5, ♭6, ♭7

What the three traditions disagree about is what makes a piece “in” one of these.

1. Music Learning Theory: mode = tonality

In Edwin Gordon’s Music Learning Theory (MLT) the word tonality is used for what most people call a mode. Gordon says tonality “best refers to what is usually called a mode,” and adds that people forget “major and minor are also modes.” He lists at least eight tonalities: major, harmonic minor, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian and Locrian (Gordon 149). Notice that harmonic minor gets its own place, separate from Aeolian.

A tonality is something you hear. It is defined by its resting tone, the note the music feels “at home” on. Gordon keeps three ideas apart (Gordon xiii, 150):

  • Tonality: the kind of home (major, Dorian, Mixolydian…), named by its resting tone in solfège.
  • Keyality: which pitch that home is on (C, G, E♭…), called the tonic. Gordon made up the word to keep it separate from:
  • Key signature: the sharps and flats you see. One sharp could be G major, E minor, A Dorian or D Mixolydian. “A key signature is seen”; keyality is heard.

“A tonality may be in any keyality and a keyality may be in any tonality” (Gordon 150): Dorian on C, Dorian on F, major on C, all different combinations.

How you name it. MLT teaches movable do with a la-based minor, so a syllable always names the same relation to the other notes. The resting tone of each tonality then gets its own syllable:

Tonality Resting tone
Major do
Minor (harmonic) and Aeolian la
Dorian re
Phrygian mi
Lydian fa
Mixolydian so
Locrian ti

The MLT question: Sing the resting tone. If you can, you have heard the tonality. You don’t need to know a scale, a key signature or a chord to answer. Music can stay in one tonality (unitonal) or move between them (multitonal), for example from harmonic minor to Mixolydian while staying in E♭ keyality (Gordon 152, 157).

The order matters in MLT: you learn to hear and sing major and minor tonalities first, then other tonalities, and only later learn their names and notation. See Audiation and the Tonal Patterns page, which has pattern sets in every tonality.

2. Classical theory: church modes, then major and minor

In classical theory, “mode” has a history with two layers.

The church modes. Medieval chant was sorted into eight modes, in four pairs. Each pair shares a final (the note a chant ends on). An authentic mode runs up an octave from the final; its plagal partner (with the prefix hypo-, as in Hypodorian) uses the same final but sits lower, with the range moved down. Today the eight are often numbered 1–8. In 1547 the Swiss theorist Heinrich Glarean, in his book Dodecachordon, added four more: Aeolian and Ionian with their plagal partners (“Mode (music)”).

Major mode and minor mode. Ionian is our major scale and Aeolian our natural minor. As the major/minor system took over, “mode” came to mean simply major mode or minor mode, and the older modes became a special colour composers reached for: the sound of the church, or of folk music (“Mode (music)”). That is why a classical textbook can say a piece in C minor is “in the minor mode,” and why mode mixture means borrowing chords from the parallel minor mode.

How a classical student finds the mode. Look at the notes used and the final (or the tonic chord), then match the pattern of whole and half steps. Two ways of learning modes are both common:

  • Relative (white-key) way: D Dorian is “C major from D to D.” Quick for spelling, but it makes Dorian sound like a part of C major.
  • Parallel way: C Dorian is “C major with ♭3 and ♭7.” This keeps the home note fixed and asks what changes, which is closer to how the mode sounds (the right-hand column of the table above).

The classical question: What scale, final and step pattern does this music use? The answer can come from the page, without playing a note, though a good analyst checks it by ear.

3. Jazz: a scale for each chord

In jazz, “mode” usually means a scale you play over one chord while it lasts. This is called chord-scale theory. When the chord changes, the scale changes.

Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook gives the method: write all the notes of the chord, including any extensions and alterations, then fill the gaps between them “with the most logical choices, avoiding augmented seconds and consecutive half steps.” His table of the usual pairs (Hutchinson, “How to Determine Chord-Scale Relationships”):

Chord Scale
CΔ7 (major seventh) C major (Ionian) or C Lydian
Cm7 C Dorian or C natural minor (Aeolian)
C7 C Mixolydian
Cø7 (half-diminished) C Locrian or C Locrian ♯2
CmΔ7 C melodic minor (ascending)
C7♯11 C Lydian dominant
C°7 C octatonic, whole–half

The jazz question: What notes sound good over this chord? Every new chord gets a new answer, named from its own root.

Same notes, three answers

Take the most common jazz progression in C major: Dm7 – G7 – CΔ7 (ii–V–I). Every chord uses only the white keys.

Dm7 G7 CΔ7
Jazz says D Dorian G Mixolydian C Ionian
Classical says ii V7 I, all in C major
MLT says one tonality, major, with do (C) as the resting tone, throughout

The jazz musician names three modes, because each is a scale built on a different chord root. Yet the notes never change. The classical and MLT answers agree here: one key, one home. For a piece to be in Dorian in the classical or MLT sense, D itself has to feel like home for the whole passage, not just for one chord.

Now the other way round: a folk tune uses only the white keys and ends on D, and the tune clearly rests on D.

  • MLT: Dorian tonality, D keyality. Resting tone re.
  • Classical: D Dorian (mode 1, authentic, if it ranges an octave up from D).
  • Jazz: a jazz player would likely hear it as a long Dm chord and play D Dorian over it. Here, for once, all three agree.

Words to keep straight

Word MLT Classical Jazz
Mode Tonality (a heard home) Scale type, church mode, or major/minor mode Scale chosen for one chord
Home note Resting tone (a syllable) and tonic (a letter) Final or tonic Chord root (changes with each chord)
Key signature Only a symbol; can’t tell you the tonality Points to a key, checked against the final Rarely used to name a mode
“Minor” Usually harmonic minor; Aeolian is separate Natural, harmonic and melodic forms of one minor mode Dorian, Aeolian or melodic minor, by chord

Try it: play a recording you know, sing the note it rests on, and decide the tonality (MLT). Then find the final and step pattern (classical). Then look at the chord symbols and name a scale for each (jazz). Where do the answers agree, and where not?
